newsitem.title: FRANCE: Valeo in safe hands for now - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Valeo in safe hands for now - analysts.

text.p: French car parts maker Valeo is in safe hands for years to come, now that holding company CGIP is buying 20 percent, but nothing rules out a merger with another car parts firm further down the line, analysts said on Tuesday.

News that CGIP is buying 20 percent from Cerus has revealed a dividend deal based on what looks like healthy profit expectations for Valeo, a healthy view of its worth and ensures continued vital ties with French carmakers, they said.
"From Valeo's point of view, it's a smart deal and everyone involved has good reason to think likewise," said one French car industry analyst.

"In five years' time it may face the same problem (question of ownership and future). The only possibility is that it would have to merge, but it would not be an acquisition (of Valeo)," the analyst added.
Industry changes and the needs for greater economies of scale was not a pressing issue at Valeo's current size.
This, he said, would be a question in perhaps five or ten years' time, or perhaps as little as three years, but not now.
CGIP is paying 330 francs a share for the stake but Valeo is paying shareholders including Cerus a special advance dividend payment of 10 francs a share later this month.

Analysts said this would be followed by another CGIP payment of 10 francs per share to Cerus if Valeo's net attributable profit after tax in 1997 came in at 1.45 billion francs ($283 million) or more.

One analyst pointed out that his estimate for profit next year had been 1.38 billion and that there was reason to believe -- because of this profit-related payout scheme -- that the result would in fact be higher.
Moreover, Valeo chairman Noel Goutard said on Tuesday the group had upped its 1996 sales expectations to 29 billion francs from 28.5 billion francs. 1995 sales were 25.23 billion francs.

Analysts said a fall in Valeo's stock price on Tuesday after the deal was detailed was probably the result of selling by speculative investors who had still been hoping the CGIP deal would fall through and that an offer from TRW or another foreign firm would emerge.
Valeo stock opened five percent lower on the Paris bourse but crept back a bit to 301.1 francs, down 3.12 percent, at 1022 GMT.
The sale to CGIP simply meant one financial investor was taking over from another and Valeo was already of a size which allowed it compete as an independent entity, analysts said.
This did not mean that the need for greater economies of scale as the industry changed over the years would not push Valeo to look for a partner in the sector.
"Today they are of a critical size but maybe in three or four years they could benefit from economies of scale in a merger," said one French analyst, asking not to be named.
"This doesn't mean they won't merge with a U.S. partner eventually," he said.
The same analyst noted that CGIP had been a shareholder in the past and knew Valeo well and that the bosses of the two companies also knew each other well in person.

French carmakers, especially PSA Peugeot Citroen, had campaigned for Valeo to stay in French hands and won French government support to try to find a French solution once it became clear the Cerus stake was up for sale.
"If Valeo had been sold to a foreign group it would have been dangerous for the French car industry," said one analyst, highlighting this threat of severing supply links with the French carmakers.
"Valeo clearly has no strategy problem. Valeo will continue to grow -- why not continue as it is with financial shareholders," he added. ($1=5.120 French Franc)
